title: From interpretation to implementation in cardiovascular care.
summary: Translating evidence into better outcomes requires both careful interpretation and effective implementation. The studies featured in this issue of Acta Cardiologica address mechanical bumping during cryoablation of atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia, myocardial infarction in young adults, prevention of contrast-induced nephropathy, intravascular imaging in left main intervention, atrial and atrioventricular remodelling in heart failure, the implementation of SGLT2 inhibitors and cardiovascular risk reduction in Belgium, successive cardiovascular risk score updates, transcatheter aortic valve implantation, and infective and rheumatic heart disease. Collectively, they show that methodological rigour and pragmatic implementation strategies remain equally essential to improve patient care.

title: Prognostic Value of the Electrical Risk Score for In-Hospital and 1-Year Mortality in Acute Decompensated Heart Failure.
summary:
BACKGROUND: The electrical risk score (ERS) integrates multiple electrocardiographic markers of cardiac electrical instability. Its prognostic role in acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) remains unknown. We evaluated the association of ERS with in-hospital and 1-year outcomes in ADHF.

METHODS: In this retrospective study, 223 patients hospitalized with ADHF were included. ERS was calculated from six ECG parameters (heart rate, LV hypertrophy, QTc, Tp-e interval, QRS transition zone, frontal QRS-T angle) and dichotomized as ERS ≥ 4 (n = 98) versus ERS ≤ 3 (n = 125). The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes were 1-year mortality and HF-related rehospitalization.

RESULTS: ERS ≥ 4 was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (9.2% vs. 1.6%, p = 0.009) and 1-year mortality (50.0% vs. 32.0%, p = 0.006). ERS ≥ 4 remained associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment for sodium and GFR (OR: 5.896, 95% CI: 1.201-28.933, p = 0.029) and with 1-year mortality after adjustment for GFR, sodium, albumin, hemoglobin, and atrial fibrillation (OR: 2.153, 95% CI: 1.163-3.985, p = 0.015). ERS alone showed modest discrimination for 1-year mortality (AUC: 0.622, p = 0.002). Adding ERS improved model fit, though the discrimination gain was modest and non-significant (DeLong p = 0.484). Rehospitalization rates did not differ between groups (52.8% vs. 45.5% in ERS ≥ 4 vs. ≤ 3, p = 0.295).

CONCLUSIONS: ERS is a simple ECG-based tool. ERS ≥ 4 was independently associated with 1-year mortality and, in an exploratory analysis, with in-hospital mortality, supporting its potential value as a complementary tool for early bedside risk stratification.

title: Cardiac Rhythm Disorders and Chronic Occupational Exposure to Pollutants: A Systematic Review.
summary: Heart rhythm disorders (arrhythmias) are a growing public health problem and can result from an imbalance in the autonomic nervous system or be exacerbated by lifestyle factors. Recent epidemiological data indicate that certain environmental factors, such as air pollution, can alter cardiac electrophysiological function. There are also conflicting findings regarding the contribution of chronic occupational exposure to toxic chemicals to arrhythmogenesis. This systematic review summarizes the available data on the associations between chronic occupational exposure to pollutants (including metals, solvents, aldehydes, amines, cyanides, plastics, acids, gases, and pesticides) and the risk of cardiac arrhythmia, and examines several hypotheses regarding their underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. Twenty-one studies were selected from several databases. During the working period, exposure to lead, carbon disulfide, certain solvents, and inhalable particles was associated with arrhythmias, specifically atrial fibrillation. Coordinated mechanisms such as cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, and inflammatory mechanisms may be involved. A preventive strategy could be implemented in factories, and practitioners could consider this explanation. These findings support the implementation of targeted preventive strategies in chemical-exposed occupational settings and warrant increased clinical vigilance for arrhythmia among exposed workers.

title: Biatrial Versus Left Atrial Maze Ablation During Cardiac Valve Surgery for Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: The ABLATION Trial.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Guidelines recommend concomitant surgical ablation during cardiac surgery in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). However, the optimal lesion set remains uncertain, with ongoing debate regarding the relative benefits and risks of biatrial versus left atrial (LA) maze ablation.

METHODS: In this multicenter, randomized, single-blind trial, patients with persistent or long-standing persistent AF undergoing rheumatic mitral valve surgery, with or without concomitant cardiac surgical procedures, were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo biatrial or LA maze ablation. The biatrial group underwent a complete Cox-Maze IV procedure; the LA group received a left-sided maze lesion set. To ensure standardization and consistency of the ablation procedures, surgeons underwent pretrial training and certification, and all procedures were videorecorded and centrally reviewed. The primary outcome was freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmias lasting >30 seconds without antiarrhythmic drugs within 12 months. The key secondary end point was freedom from permanent pacemaker implantation.

RESULTS: All 323 randomized patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (mean age, 56.5 years; 72.1% women; mean LA diameter, 51.9 mm). At 12 months, 78.7% of patients (129 of 164) in the biatrial group and 68.6% (109 of 159) in the LA group were free from atrial tachyarrhythmias (adjusted difference, 10.7% [1-sided lower 95% CI, 3%]; P=0.01). Freedom from permanent pacemaker implantation was noted in 97.0% (159 of 164) of the biatrial group and 98.1% (156 of 159) of the LA group, meeting the predefined noninferiority criterion with a margin of -5% (adjusted difference, -1.1% [1-sided lower 95% CI, -3.9%]; Pnoninferiority=0.01).

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with persistent or long-standing persistent AF undergoing rheumatic cardiac valve surgery, biatrial maze ablation was superior to LA maze ablation in reducing recurrent atrial tachyarrhythmias, while maintaining noninferiority with respect to permanent pacemaker implantation. These findings provide direct evidence to inform lesion-set selection for surgical ablation during cardiac surgery.

REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT05021601.

title: Surgical Treatment of Atrial Fibrillation.
summary: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with an increased risk of stroke, heart failure, mortality, and reduced quality of life. Although catheter ablation is the most widely used rhythm control strategy, its efficacy is limited in patients with non-paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and large left atria. To address this therapeutic gap, surgical approaches, including minimally invasive ablation, hybrid epicardial-endocardial strategies, and left atrial appendage exclusion, have continued to evolve. In this review, we focus on recent evidence to guide clinical decision-making on patient selection, advances in minimally invasive surgical and hybrid techniques, left atrial appendage exclusion, and postoperative anticoagulation management. Minimally invasive standalone Cox-Maze IV procedure and hybrid epicardial-endocardial ablation have demonstrated superior long-term freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmias compared with thoracoscopic epicardial surgical ablation or catheter ablation alone. Five-year arrhythmia-free survival has approached 85% to 95% in experienced centers after the Cox-Maze IV procedure and approximately 60% to 70% after hybrid ablation, compared with 35% to 45% after thoracoscopic epicardial ablation and 30% to 35% after single catheter ablation alone. Surgical left atrial appendage exclusion performed at the time of ablation may further reduce thromboembolic risk, although the optimal strategy for postprocedural anticoagulation remains uncertain. Careful patient selection remains essential, with atrial fibrillation type, duration, left atrial size, and previous treatment failure known to be key predictors of procedural success. As surgical techniques and supporting evidence continue to grow, standalone surgical ablation may assume a more important role in the contemporary management of atrial fibrillation, particularly for patients with advanced disease who are unlikely to achieve durable rhythm control with catheter ablation alone.

title: Initial Experience with Bachmann Bundle Pacing Lead Implantation as a Rhythm Control Strategy in Atrial Fibrillation.
summary:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Bachmann bundle pacing (BBP) is challenging during atrial fibrillation (AF) because ECG based endpoints cannot confirm lead positioning. We aimed to demonstrate the feasibility of a practical approach to BBP implantation during AF and propose a framework for comprehensive conduction system pacing with BBP and left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) for rhythm control in patients referred for pace-and-ablate therapy.

METHODS AND RESULTS: Twenty-four consecutive patients with persistent or longstanding persistent AF and preserved ejection fraction underwent dual-chamber BBP and LBBP implantation with individually optimized pacing rate and AV interval. Twelve underwent BBP during AF (Group 1) and 12 during sinus (Group 2), including six cardioverted intraprocedurally. During AF, lead positioning was guided by anatomical landmarks, local electrograms, current of injury, and impedance changes. After sinus rhythm restoration, BBP was confirmed in 11/12 Group 1 patients. Reductions in P-wave duration and interatrial block were observed in both groups. Seventeen had been referred for pace-and-ablate therapy; three in Group 1 reverted spontaneously to sinus rhythm before cardioversion. Over a median 192 [139-212] days after sinus restoration, 12/17 maintained sinus rhythm; 2 underwent AV node ablation, 1 AF ablation, 1 repeat cardioversion, and 1 required rate-control medication for paroxysmal AF. No complications occurred.

CONCLUSION: BBP implantation during AF is feasible using anatomical and electrophysiological markers, with Bachmann bundle capture confirmed after sinus rhythm restoration. Exploratory findings suggest that comprehensive conduction system pacing with BBP and LBBP may support a rhythm-control (pace-and-wait) strategy in persistent AF patients referred for pace-and-ablate therapy.

title: Left atrial pressure and arrhythmia recurrence after pulmonary vein isolation - more than a dichotomous threshold.
Predictors and Long-term Prognosis of Silent Cerebral Embolism After Catheter Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation.
Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation in adults with advanced kidney disease: UK kidney association clinical practice guideline.
summary: Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have an increased risk of developing atrial fibrillation (AF). CKD is also associated with an increased risk of stroke and systemic embolism (SSE). Despite the increased thromboembolic risk associated with CKD and AF, patients with advanced CKD simultaneously have a higher risk of bleeding. Following results from large randomised controlled trials prophylaxis of thromboembolic events from atrial fibrillation (AF) has shifted from vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). However, trials of DOACs excluded patients with advanced kidney disease (CrCl < 30 ml/min), therefore good-quality data are limited in this population. This leads to decision-making around anticoagulation difficult. In those with advanced kidney disease, especially those on dialysis, there is limited data on the efficacy of anticoagulants for AF in terms of stroke reduction. There are ongoing studies to determine efficacy of anticoagulants in reducing the risk of thromboembolic stroke and systemic embolism in this population. These UK Kidney Association (UKKA) guidelines, which have been endorsed by the British Cardiovascular Society, provide best-practice guidance on the use of anticoagulants for atrial fibrillation in the context of advanced CKD. There are recommendations about the option of no anticoagulation, the use of DOACs, the monitoring of anticoagulants and the use of left atrial appendage occlusion. It also includes research recommendations.

title: Preoperative C‑reactive protein‑to‑albumin ratio as a predictor of postoperative atrial fibrillation after coronary artery bypass grafting.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) is a common complication after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), leading to higher rates of morbidity and greater demands on healthcare resources. This study aimed to assess the relationship between the C-reactive protein to albumin ratio (CAR) and the development of POAF in patients undergoing CABG.

METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 109 patients who underwent elective CABG. CAR was measured preoperatively. The primary outcome was the incidence of POAF within the first postoperative week. Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were used to evaluate the predictive value of CAR and other clinical variables.

RESULTS: POAF occurred in 29 patients (26.6%). The mean CAR was significantly higher in the POAF group, with ROC analysis demonstrating excellent discriminatory ability (AUC = 0.9713, cut-off = 1.44). Additionally, CAR showed a moderate ability to predict mortality (AUC = 0.698, cut-off = 2.27), a novel finding not extensively reported in prior studies. The odds of developing POAF increased by 50% for each unit increase in CAR (OR: 1.50; 95% CI: 1.20, 1.88; p = 0.001), reinforcing its potential as a biomarker for risk stratification.

CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative CAR is a strong, independent predictor of POAF after CABG. Incorporating CAR into routine risk assessment may help identify high-risk patients and guide prophylactic strategies.

title: Electrophysiological Markers in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Enhancing Sudden Cardiac Death Risk Prediction with Index of Cardiac Electrophysiological Balance and Its Corrected Variant
summary: Background Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is characterized by asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy and myocardial fibrosis, which significantly increases the risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD). Existing risk stratification models are limited in predicting SCD risk in patients within the "gray zone"-those with intermediate risk. This study investigates the prognostic utility of the Index of Cardiac Electrophysiological Balance (ICEB) and its corrected variant (ICEBc) in predicting ventricular arrhythmias (VAs) in HCM. To evaluate the predictive value of ICEB and ICEBc for Life-Threatening Arrhythmias (LTA) and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) in HCM and compare their performance with traditional repolarization parameters and the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) SCD Risk Score.Methods A retrospective observational study was conducted at a single center, including 127 HCM patients categorized into 3 groups: LTA (n = 45), NSVT (n = 29), and control (n = 53). Electrocardiographic parameters, including ICEB, ICEBc, Tp-e interval, Tp-e/QTc ratio, and QRS-T angle were measured. Multiple logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of VAs.Results The ICEB and ICEBc were significantly lower in LTA and NSVT groups compared to the control group (P < .001), indicating increased arrhythmogenic risk. The ROC curve analysis showed that ICEB and ICEBc had superior predictive power for LTA and NSVT compared to traditional markers and the ESC SCD Risk Score, with the highest area under the curve (AUC) for the Base + ICEB Model (AUC = 0.79).Conclusion The ICEB and ICEBc are robust markers of repolarization heterogeneity and effective predictors of VAs in HCM patients. Their integration into existing risk stratification models could enhance predictive accuracy, particularly for gray zone patients.

title: Successful percutaneous intervention for post-operative coronary artery stenosis in a child: a case report.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for coronary artery stenosis in young children is rare, and evidence guiding management remains limited. Established indications for PCI in children include reversing or preventing ischaemia, as well as preventing sudden cardiac death. Guidance on optimal revascularization approaches and long-term outcomes remains underreported. We report successful PCI for significant post-operative right coronary artery (RCA) stenosis in a 7-year-old.

CASE SUMMARY: The patient presented with acute onset cardiac failure aged 5 years. Echocardiography demonstrated aneurysmal aortic root dilatation with severe aortic regurgitation and left ventricular dysfunction. The aetiology was found to be infectious, and the patient underwent aortic root replacement. The postoperative course was complicated by myocardial ischaemia and right ventricular dysfunction, necessitating RCA re-implantation before discharge. At age 7, although asymptomatic, follow-up imaging demonstrated progressive proximal RCA stenosis. Stress cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed inducible perfusion defects, and exercise testing confirmed dynamic ECG changes consistent with ischaemia. Selective coronary angiography demonstrated critical proximal RCA stenosis. In collaboration with adult interventional cardiologists, PCI with coronary stent implantation was performed successfully, restoring coronary perfusion and improving functional capacity.

DISCUSSION: This case highlights the feasibility of PCI with coronary stenting for complex post-operative coronary stenosis in paediatric patients. Input from adult interventional cardiologists allowed for technical challenges to be navigated and resulted in restoration of coronary perfusion with substantial improvements to patient quality of life.

title: Sex-specific challenges and psychosocial adaptation in women with implantable cardioverter defibrillators.
summary: Although cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death in women globally, it is underdiagnosed and undertreated. Implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICDs) reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death, but many women report diminished quality of life and avoidance behaviors and present sex-specific challenges postimplantation. Women have higher rates of concern, comorbidities, psychological distress, and anatomic factors that can affect the outcomes of ICD therapy. Women experience more ICD-related complications, psychological distress, and body image concerns, which can adversely affect their quality of life and ICD implant adjustments. Anatomic differences and comorbidities may contribute to these issues. Despite these factors, women remain underrepresented in clinical trials and receive ICD therapy less often than men. Psychosocial interventions such as education, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and support groups have shown promise in improving outcomes, but further research is required to assess their effectiveness. Although current interventions show potential, persistent disparities in utilization and research underscore the need for sex-specific strategies. This article explores sex-specific challenges and outcomes associated with ICD therapy in women, and highlights opportunities for tailored interventions to improve quality of life, sexual health, and well-being.

title: Causal Peak Refinement Reduces Timing Error of a Classical R-Peak Detector Across Beat Morphologies
summary: Abstract Purpose Classical ECG R-peak detectors are usually reported with a single aggregate score, which can hide failures on unusual beats and under noise. One such detector was evaluated by beat type, noise type and matching tolerance, and a refinement stage was tested. Methods A simplified Pan-Tompkins-style detector and a causal peak-refinement stage, which reassigns each detection to the largest absolute-amplitude sample of the 5–15 Hz band-passed signal within ± 50 ms, were implemented in Simulink. Nine MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database records (first 120 s each) were used: five to choose settings and four held out. Noise from the MIT-BIH Noise Stress Test Database was added at 24, 12, 6 and 0 dB. Results At ± 50 ms the baseline’s mean F1 was 92.5% (88.1% on a right bundle branch block record and 63.4% on a paced record), but it was 98.2% at ± 75 ms, indicating mainly timing errors. Refinement reduced the mean absolute timing error from 25.8 ms to 6.0 ms and raised the ± 50 ms mean F1 to 98.0%. Refined F1 was equal or higher on all four held-out records. Electrode motion at 0 dB was the hardest noise (tuning records: mean F1 87.3% baseline, 91.7% refined). Refinement did not help record 207, which contains ventricular flutter and unmatched premature ventricular contractions (F1 86.3%). Conclusion Most errors under the ± 50 ms matching criterion were timing errors, and a simple causal refinement stage reduced them. The results come from nine short records and one detector, and they do not rank detectors.

title: PREGNANCY OUTCOMES IN A CONTEMPORARY COHORT OF WOMEN WITH REPAIRED TETRALOGY OF FALLOT.
authors: Inara Alarcon de la Lastra Cubiles
summary: Most women with repaired Tetralogy of Fallot (rTOF) now reach reproductive age, but pregnancy outcomes in contemporary cohorts, particularly after pulmonary valve replacement (PVR), remain uncertain. The aim of this study as to assess maternal cardiac, obstetric and neonatal outcomes in a contemporary cohort of women with rTOF. We retrospectively included all pregnancies in women with rTOF followed at a tertiary referral center for complex congenital heart disease (CHD) and high-risk pregnancy between 2013 and 2024. A total of 44 pregnancies in 32 women with rTOF were included, resulting in 45 live births. Severe PR was present in 43% of pregnancies, and 40% had undergone prior PVR. Maternal cardiac events occurred in 6.8%: 2 cases of supraventricular arrhythmias and 1 case of thrombosis on an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) lead. Among women with prior PVR, transvalvular gradients increased transiently during pregnancy and returned to baseline postpartum. Mean gestational age was 38 weeks, vaginal birth was preferred and cesarean section was performed in 18% of pregnancies. The most frequent adverse obstetric and neonatal outcomes were low birth weight (22%) and preterm birth (11%), both associated with lower pre-pregnancy right ventricular ejection fraction (RVEF) possibly reflecting impaired uteroplacental perfusion related to right ventricular dysfunction. In conclusion, in this contemporary cohort, pregnancy in women with rTOF was associated with low risk of maternal cardiac events, mainly supraventricular arrhythmias. However, low birth weight and preterm birth remained frequent and were associated with lower pre-pregnancy RVEF, underscoring the importance of specialized cardio-obstetric follow-up.

title: Diabetes mellitus and the risk of sudden cardiac death in patients with and without coronary artery disease.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Diabetes is associated with sudden cardiac death (SCD), but evidence in patients without coronary artery disease (CAD) remains limited. SCD risk may vary by revascularisation strategy in diabetic patients with CAD.

METHODS: We retrospectively analysed 22,395 consecutive patients undergoing coronary angiography from 2007 to 2018, either electively for suspected or known CAD or for acute coronary syndrome. Follow-up ended 31 December 2022. Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA), SCD and SCD-equivalent events were adjudicated using medical records, death certificates, and nationwide mortality data.

RESULTS: Among 22,395 patients, 5,804 had diabetes. Over a median follow-up of 8.1 years (IQR 5.1-11.6), 1,710 experienced SCA, including 1,046 SCD or SCD-equivalent events. After multivariable adjustment including left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), diabetes showed similar associations with SCD or SCD-equivalent event (subdistribution hazard ratio [SHR] 1.38, 1.21-1.58; P < 0.001) and non-SCD death (SHR 1.37, 1.30-1.44; P < 0.001). Yet, among patients with diabetes, the 10-year cumulative incidence of non-SCA death was more than three times that of SCA. Diabetes was associated with SCD or SCD-equivalent event even without obstructive CAD (SHR 1.53, 1.11-2.12; P = 0.010). In patients with diabetes and CAD, lower SCD risk was observed in revascularized patients than in those receiving medical therapy (SHR 0.77, 0.60-0.99; P = 0.039). The diabetes-SCD association appeared stronger at age < 70 years, with LVEF ≥ 40%, in type 1 diabetes, and with higher HbA1c levels.

CONCLUSIONS: Diabetes was associated with SCD irrespective of obstructive CAD, but the high competing burden of non-SCA death highlights the challenge of SCA prevention and the importance of identifying higher-risk subgroups among patients with diabetes.

title: Refractory ventricular tachyarrhythmia following a suicidal massive caffeine overdose: a case report and review of emergency management.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Caffeine is one of the most widely consumed psychoactive substances worldwide and is readily accessible in tablet formulations and caffeinated beverages. Although moderate caffeine intake is generally considered safe, massive acute ingestion can result in severe toxicity involving the central nervous and cardiovascular systems. Life-threatening manifestations include seizures, profound electrolyte disturbances, metabolic derangements, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias. Because caffeine has favorable dialyzable properties, including low molecular weight, low protein binding, and a relatively small volume of distribution, extracorporeal toxin removal may play a critical therapeutic role in severe intoxication refractory to conventional supportive and antiarrhythmic management.

CASE PRESENTATION: We report the case of a previously healthy 16-year-old Iranian adolescent girl who intentionally ingested 10.8 g of caffeine in a suicide attempt. Approximately two hours after ingestion, she presented with markedly reduced consciousness, agitation, generalized tremor, intermittent tonic/myoclonic seizure-like activity, sinus tachycardia (180-190 beats/min), hypokalemia (serum potassium 2.7 mEq/L), primary metabolic acidosis, significant rhabdomyolysis, and electrocardiographic abnormalities including mild QRS widening and QTc prolongation (~ 500 ms). Urine toxicology screening was positive for caffeine, supporting the diagnosis in conjunction with the clear ingestion history and subsequent patient confirmation. Despite early airway protection, gastrointestinal decontamination, electrolyte and acid-base correction, dual antiarrhythmic therapy with amiodarone and lidocaine, and repeated synchronized electrical cardioversion, she developed recurrent refractory sustained ventricular tachycardia, transient progression to asystole requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and persistent severe metabolic instability. Emergency intermittent hemodialysis was initiated approximately 3-4 h after emergency department arrival, resulting in rapid correction of metabolic acidosis, complete cessation of malignant ventricular arrhythmias, and sustained restoration of stable sinus rhythm. The patient subsequently demonstrated progressive neurological recovery without persistent cardiac or neurological sequelae.

CONCLUSION: This case highlights the potentially catastrophic cardiovascular consequences of massive caffeine intoxication and emphasizes the importance of early recognition, aggressive supportive care, rapid correction of metabolic abnormalities, and timely escalation to extracorporeal toxin removal in refractory cases. In patients with persistent malignant ventricular arrhythmias despite optimized pharmacologic and electrical management, intermittent hemodialysis may represent a life-saving therapeutic intervention capable of rapidly reversing toxicity and improving clinical outcomes.

title: Best Evidence Summary of Phase II Exercise-Based Cardiac Rehabilitation for Patients with Dilated Cardiomyopathy After Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy.
summary:
BACKGROUND: This study aimed to systematically summarize the available evidence on Phase II exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation (CR) for patients with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) after cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), so as to provide an evidence-based framework for clinical nursing practice.

METHODS: A comprehensive computerized search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, Web of Science, CNKI, WanFang, VIP, and SinoMed, as well as guideline repositories, evidence-based databases, and professional association websites. The included document types were clinical decisions, guidelines, expert consensus or consensus documents, evidence summaries and systematic reviews.

RESULTS: Twenty-eight publications were included: 2 clinical decisions, 10 guidelines, 1 systematic review, 11 expert consensus or consensus documents and 4 evidence summaries. A total of 42 pieces of evidence items were summarized across 12 themes: multidisciplinary collaboration, indications and contraindications for exercise rehabilitation, pre-exercise assessment, pre-exercise preparation, exercise prescription, aerobic exercise, resistance training; pulmonary rehabilitation training, flexibility training, personalized adjustment, remote supervision and support, and emergency management.

CONCLUSION: This study synthesized available evidence on Phase II exercise-based CR for patients with DCM after CRT. Most included evidence was derived from broader heart failure or cardiac rehabilitation populations; direct evidence specific to DCM after CRT remains limited. These findings may inform the development of individualized rehabilitation protocols, but recommendations should be applied with caution.

REGISTRATION: This evidence summary was registered with the Fudan University Center for Evidence-Based Nursing (Registration No. ES202610091).

title: Conduction system pacing vs biventricular pacing in heart failure patients undergoing cardiac resynchronization therapy: an updated grade-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared conduction system pacing (CSP) with biventricular pacing (BVP) for cardiac resynchronization therapy in heart failure.

METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ScienceDirect were searched from inception through 16 May 2026 for randomized trials. Random-effects Mean Difference/Odds Ratio and Peto pooling were performed with Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 and GRADE assessment.

RESULTS: Twelve trials (1,152 patients) were included. CSP shortened QRS duration (mean difference [MD] -10.03 ms, 95% confidence interval [CI] -15.95 to -4.12) and increased absolute left ventricular ejection fraction at 6 months (MD 3.67% points, 95% CI 1.38-5.95). Six-month change was not significantly different (MD 2.07% points, 95% CI -0.66 to 4.80); 12-month improvement favored BVP (MD -3.28% points, 95% CI -5.00 to -1.55). Mortality (risk ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.33-1.48), heart failure hospitalization (Peto odds ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.47-2.33), and pneumothorax (Peto odds ratio 1.94, 95% CI 0.20-18.71) did not differ significantly.

CONCLUSIONS: CSP showed physiological benefits without established clinical superiority. Heterogeneity, small trials, and limited follow-up restrict interpretation.

REVIEW REGISTRATION: International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO): CRD420261413053. Registry: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/.

title: Intraoperative Recognition and Management of Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy Defibrillator Lead Dysfunction During Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation.
Early Left Bundle Branch Pacing for Complete Left Bundle Branch Block and Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction of 36%-50%: The EARLY-RESYNC Randomized Trial.
summary:
AIMS: To compare the effects of early resynchronization with left bundle branch pacing (early-LBBP) versus guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) alone on cardiac function in patients with complete left bundle branch block (CLBBB) and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 36%-50%.

METHODS AND RESULTS: In this prospective, randomized, multicenter trial, 37 patients (mean age 60.5 ± 12.3 years, male 40.5%, LVEF 42.6% ± 6.0%) were assigned to early-LBBP plus GDMT (n=19) or GDMT alone (n=18). The primary endpoint was the between-group difference in the change of LVEF from baseline to 6 months. Secondary endpoints included changes in echocardiographic parameters and clinical outcomes. Analyses were performed according to the intention-to-treat principle. At 6-month follow-up, the adjusted mean improvement in LVEF was greater in the early-LBBP group than in the GDMT group (mean difference: 7.4%, 95% CI: 1.9 to 12.9%; P =0.013), with consistent findings in the per-protocol analysis. Early-LBBP was also associated with a greater reduction in LV end-systolic volume (-23.6mL; 95% CI: -42.3 to -4.8ml) and a higher rate of final LVEF ≥50% (78.9% vs. 38.9%) at 6 months compared with GDMT alone.

CONCLUSION: In patients with CLBBB and LVEF 36%-50%, LBBP combined with GDMT resulted in greater improvement in LVEF at 6 months than GDMT alone. Larger randomized trials are needed to establish its long-term clinical benefits and optimal timing.

title: KRT16 From Diverse Tumors Induces Atrial Remodeling and Fibrillation via Endothelial-to-Mesenchymal Transition.
summary: Anticancer therapy increases the incidence of atrial fibrillation (AF), the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia worldwide. However, whether multiple cancers directly promote AF independently of anticancer therapy through shared mechanisms remains unclear. Here, retrospective clinical analyses revealed significantly increased AF prevalence in pre-treatment female patients with breast cancer (BC), lung cancer (LC), and colorectal cancer (CRC), independent of anticancer therapy. Consistently, orthotopic tumor-bearing mouse models exhibited enhanced AF inducibility accompanied by atrial enlargement, fibrosis, and electrical remodeling. Integrated transcriptomic analyses, combined with the TCGA datasets, identified endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) as a shared atrial remodeling pathway underlying tumor-associated AF across multiple cancers. Mechanistically, keratin 16 (KRT16) acted as a shared circulating factor across multiple malignancies. KRT16 accumulated in atrial endothelial cells and promoted EndMT through annexin A2 (AnxA2)-dependent activation of TGF-β1/Smad signaling. KRT16 promoted abnormal membrane retention of AnxA2 by suppressing Tyr23 phosphorylation, thereby sustaining profibrotic signaling and atrial remodeling. Genetic silencing of KRT16 in cancer cells or endothelial knockdown of AnxA2 markedly attenuated EndMT, atrial fibrosis, and AF susceptibility in tumor-bearing mice. Our findings demonstrate that multiple cancers directly induce atrial remodeling and AF through a shared mechanism centered on KRT16-driven EndMT, identifying this pathway as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Novel markers for atrial substrate characterization: implications on atrial fibrillation risk stratification.
summary:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Atrial fibrillation is increasingly recognized as a manifestation of an underlying atrial disease process that is incompletely captured by conventional temporal classification. This review examines established and emerging markers of atrial substrate and their potential role in atrial fibrillation risk stratification.

RECENT FINDINGS: Electrocardiographic indices, left atrial volumetric and strain measures, computed tomography-derived left atrial wall characteristics, late gadolinium enhancement and flow assessment by cardiac magnetic resonance, high-density electroanatomic mapping, circulating biomarkers and genetic profiling provide complementary measures of electrical, structural, mechanical and hemodynamic remodelling. Recent studies have refined noninvasive identification of low-voltage substrate and risk stratification of atrial fibrillation progression and complications, evaluated substrate-guided ablation strategies, and expanded understanding of the prognostic significance of emerging substrate markers.

SUMMARY: Multimodal atrial substrate characterization may improve prediction of atrial fibrillation onset and progression, thromboembolic complications and outcomes after rhythm-control therapy. Clinical translation requires standardized acquisition and analytical methods, reproducible thresholds, prospective validation of integrated risk models, and prospective trials demonstrating improved outcomes with substrate-guided management.

title: Severe neonatal long QT syndrome type 3 treated with genotype-directed therapy and early left cardiac sympathetic denervation: a case report.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Long QT syndrome type 3 may present in foetal or neonatal life with QT prolongation, 2:1 atrioventricular (AV) block, and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias. Early recognition and individualizes genotype-directed management may be lifesaving.

CASE SUMMARY: A neonate delivered after foetal bradycardia and intermittent 2:1 AV block presented with severe QT prolongation and recurrent torsades de pointes. The functional 2:1 AV block persisted despite beta-blockade and magnesium administration. Because of recurrent ventricular arrhythmias, video-assisted thoracoscopic left cardiac sympathetic denervation (LCSD) and implantable loop recorder were performed on Day 8 of life. Genetic testing identified a de novo likely pathogenic SCN5A_p.(Ala1656Val) missense variant. Subsequent lidocaine testing demonstrated marked QT shortening, supporting sodium channel-mediated disease and guiding treatment with mexiletine and flecainide. Long-term follow-up required implantable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy, but arrhythmic burden progressively improved.

DISCUSSION: This case supports the potential role of early multimodal treatment in malignant neonatal long QT syndrome type 3, combining LCSD, continuous rhythm monitoring, and genotype-directed sodium channel blockade.

title: Aspirin Use May Increase Atrial Fibrillation Risk: A Mendelian Randomization Analysis.
summary:
PURPOSE: The relationship between aspirin use and atrial fibrillation (AF) remains uncertain. This study is aimed at determining the causal association of aspirin use and AF risk by Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis.

METHODS: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) for aspirin use and AF were obtained from genome-wide association studies (GWAS). The inverse variance weighted (IVW) was used as the primary MR analysis method. In addition, I performed Cochran's Q, MR-Egger's intercept, leave-one-out, MR-PRESSO, and Radial MR to evaluate heterogeneity, horizontal pleiotropy, sensitivity, and reliability of the results.

RESULTS: Finally, 42 independent SNPs were selected as instrumental variables (IVs). The findings revealed that genetically proxied aspirin use elevated AF risk (odds ratio [OR]IVW = 1.96 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.10, 3.47], p = 0.021) in European population. The subsequent analysis confirmed the validity of the primary MR results. Cochran's Q test (p > 0.05), MR-Egger's intercept (p > 0.05), MR-PRESSO global test (p > 0.05), and Radial MR (p > 0.05).

CONCLUSION: This MR study provides evidence suggesting a potential causal association between aspirin use and an increased risk of AF. However, given the inherent limitations of the MR design, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Future large-scale randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with long-term follow-up are warranted to confirm and extend these observations.

title: Sex Differences in QT Interval and Beat-to-Beat Temporal QT Variability at Rest and After Submaximal Exercise in Young Adults With and Without Obesity: A Cross-Sectional Study.
summary: Background Obesity increases arrhythmia risk by altering QT dynamics. However, sex-specific differences during rest and exercise remain insufficiently characterized in young adults, representing a critical gap in cardiovascular risk research. Objectives This study aimed to (1) evaluate sex differences and the potential interaction between sex and obesity in heart rate-corrected QT interval (QTc) and single-lead temporal beat-to-beat QT variability (QTvar) at rest and following submaximal exercise and (2) explore subgroup-specific relationships between body mass index (BMI) and repolarization parameters. Methods A cross-sectional observational study was conducted on 200 healthy young adults (aged 18-25 years) categorized into obese and non-obese groups based on World Health Organization Asia-Pacific BMI criteria. Participants underwent resting and post-exercise (50% VO2max) continuous Lead II electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings following a standardized submaximal treadmill protocol. QTc (using Bazett's formula) and temporal beat-to-beat QTvar (QTvar = QTmax - QTmin across 10 consecutive complexes) were quantified from Lead II. Statistical comparisons with Bonferroni adjustments and correlation analyses between BMI and QT parameters were performed. Results Obese females demonstrated significantly higher resting QTvar values than obese males both at rest (227.2 ± 68.5 vs. 174.6 ± 57.2 ms, p = 0.0002, Cohen's d = 0.83) and post-exercise (214.0 ± 25.4 vs. 184.6 ± 81.6 ms, p = 0.045, Cohen's d = 0.48). QTc intervals were numerically longer in females across groups, though differences were not statistically significant (p > 0.05). Following Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons across correlation analyses (α = 0.0031), a significant positive correlation between BMI and post-exercise QTc was observed in obese females (r = 0.572, p = 0.0004), whereas correlations between BMI and resting QTc in females (r = 0.402, p = 0.018) and recovery QTc in obese males (r = 0.370, p = 0.005) represented exploratory associations that did not meet strict multiplicity adjustment. Conclusions Obese young females exhibit greater temporal beat-to-beat QTvar than obese males, suggesting sex-specific differences in dynamic ventricular repolarization stability under conditions of elevated adiposity. The emergence of a robust positive correlation between BMI and recovery QTc in obese females highlights the potential for differential autonomic and electrophysiological responses following physical exertion, providing hypothesis-generating evidence that warrants prospective longitudinal study.
